title: Liberation (1945)
hookLine: the camps are liberated, and survivors face a world that is gone

cards: Soldiers push open a gate. They came to fight a war, and nothing prepared them for what's inside: people too thin to stand, barracks full of the sick, a silence that doesn't sound like peace.
On the other side of the gate, a prisoner hears that the guards are gone. Free. And almost at once, a second question arrives behind the first.
Free to go where? To whom? Is anyone left?
Today's word is the first half of that moment. I'll hold the second half too.

teach.b: As the Allied armies crossed Europe, they reached the camps one after another: Soviet soldiers in the east, at places like Majdanek and Auschwitz; American and British soldiers in the west, at Buchenwald, Dachau, Bergen-Belsen.
What they found, they photographed and filmed, and commanders ordered it recorded, so no one could later say it hadn't happened. Liberation did not end the suffering at once.
Soldiers handed out their own rations out of plain kindness, chocolate, tinned meat, but starving bodies could not take rich food, and some who lived to see the gates open died in the days after.
Doctors and nurses learned to feed people slowly. Then came the second question. Survivors went looking for family.

teach.h: NAMES ON LISTS, NAMES ON WALLS.
teach.b: They read lists, posted lists, wrote names on walls, asked every stranger from their town. Some walked home to find no one waiting and strangers living in their houses. And in the middle of all this, something else.
At Bergen-Belsen, in the days after the British arrived, a Jewish army chaplain led a Sabbath service among the barracks. Survivors sang, and their voices were recorded.
A psalm describes a return from exile in just this strange way: "When the LORD brought back those that returned to Zion, we were like unto them that dream."
For those who lived it, liberation could feel like that: real, and not yet believable. The word means being set free. It doesn't mean being made whole.

how: Jewish communities remember the liberation of the camps on Yom HaShoah and at memorial services, and some survivors and their families mark the day their own camp was liberated.

games.q: you're a soldier who has just opened a camp. starving prisoners reach toward you. you have your rations: chocolate, tinned meat. what do you do?
games.why: soldiers did hand out their rations, out of kindness, and some starving people couldn't take the rich food. doctors and nurses learned to feed people slowly.

practice: You don't need any picture of the camps.

Think of one survivor walking out through a gate, and hold that person gently, with the first ordinary things that came after: a bowl of soup, a clean shirt, a letter, a name found on a list, and if you know a survivor's name or a family story, bring it in.
If you pray, pray for the survivors and for those who carry their memory; if not, simply keep them company in your mind.

wordCard.voice: Liberation. Being set free: the opening of the camps as the war in Europe ended, and the first slow steps of the people inside.

orig.note: Hebrew: freedom. Passover is called the season of our freedom.

carryVoice: Your line: set free, not yet whole. Both halves are part of the story. Until tomorrow.
